items.new: I protested my innocence. I could see that behind the mask of these half-humorous insinuations, this old seaman, as an insulated, Quakerish Nantucketer, was full of his insular prejudices. He was rather suspicious of all outsiders unless they came from Cape Cod or the Vineyard.

items.new: But one thing, nevertheless, made me a little uneasy about getting a generous share of the profits. Ashore, I had heard about both Captain Peleg and his strange old crony Bildad — how, being the principal owners of the Pequod, the other, lesser and scattered owners left nearly all management of the ship's business to these two. And for all I knew, stingy old Bildad might have a great deal of say in hiring the crew, especially since I now found him aboard the Pequod, completely at home in the cabin, reading his Bible as if by his own fireside. While Peleg was vainly trying to sharpen a pen with his jackknife, old Bildad — to my considerable surprise, given that he was such an interested party in these proceedings — paid us no attention at all. He just went on mumbling to himself from his book: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth —"

items.reason: Source: 'And all this seemed natural enough; especially as in the merchant service many captains never show themselves...'. The candidate splits this into two sentences and drops 'especially as', so the merchant-service custom no longer reads as the reason it seemed natural.
items.new: How about that! Here at the very moment of departure, Captain Peleg and Captain Bildad were running the show on the quarter-deck, just as if they were going to be the joint commanders at sea as well as, to all appearances, in port. As for Captain Ahab, there was still no sign of him. They said he was in the cabin. But the idea was that his presence wasn't at all necessary for getting the ship underway and steering her well out to sea. That was really the pilot's job, and since he hadn't fully recovered — so they said — Captain Ahab stayed below. All of this seemed natural enough, especially since in the merchant service many captains never show themselves on deck for some time after the anchor is raised, but stay at the cabin table having a farewell party with their shore friends before those friends leave the ship for good with the pilot.

items.reason: Accessibility edit introduced a mis-paired dash. Source: 'For loath to depart, yet; very loath to leave, for good, a ship bound on so long and perilous a voyage—beyond both stormy Capes; a ship in which...'. The candidate's '...just yet — very loath ... voyage — beyond both stormy Capes' makes the two dashes read as a parenthesis, so 'beyond both stormy Capes' attaches to 'depart just yet'. The inserted 'he was' also turns the fronted participial series into a main clause, leaving '— poor old Bildad lingered long' as a second, run-on clause. Fix restores the source's structure (loath...; loath... — poor old Bildad lingered long) with the dash only where the source has it.
items.new: It was curious, and not unpleasing, how Peleg and Bildad were affected at this point, especially Captain Bildad. For, loath to depart just yet, very loath to leave for good a ship bound on so long and perilous a voyage — beyond both stormy Capes; a ship in which some thousands of his hard-earned dollars were invested; a ship in which an old shipmate sailed as captain, a man almost as old as himself, setting out once more to meet all the terrors of the pitiless jaw; loath to say goodbye to a thing so brimful in every way of every interest to him — poor old Bildad lingered long. He paced the deck with anxious strides; ran down into the cabin to speak another farewell word there; came on deck again and looked to windward; looked toward the wide and endless waters, bounded only by the far-off, unseen Eastern Continents; looked toward the land; looked aloft; looked right and left; looked everywhere and nowhere; and at last, mechanically coiling a rope on its pin, he convulsively grasped stout Peleg by the hand and, holding up a lantern, stood for a moment gazing heroically into his face, as much as to say, "Nevertheless, friend Peleg, I can stand it; yes, I can."
